In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding how the brain controls its own activity, and how the brain's own activity can go wrong, leading to disease.
how the release of neurotransmitters is controlled by the activity of the neurons that secrete them.
the mechanisms underlying the release of dopamine from the cell bodies and dendritic processes of dopamine neurons in the brain.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
somatodendritally released DA is Ca2+ dependent but does not require vesicular release.
somatodendritc release of DA is not yet fully understood, but it is clear that it is not a simple passive process, and that it is a complex process with many components and steps.
somatodendritc DA release is a Ca2+ dependent process, which involves a combination of vesicular release and non-vesicular release mechanisms.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
somatodendritally released dopamine is Ca(2+)-dependent.
the somatodendritric DA release is Ca2+ dependent and that the release is mediated by a vesicle exocytosis.

the release of dopamine from the somatodendrites of dopaminergic neurons depends on Ca2+ influx through L-type Ca2+ channels, and that this release is regulated by the vesicular monoamine transporter-2 (VMAT-2) and the vesicular glutamate transporter-2 (VGLUT-2), which are both present in dopaminergic neurons.
The main takeaway from our work is that
somatodendritc release is Ca2+ dependent, and that the Ca2+ source for release can be local or global.
somatodendritc DA release is not a passive process, but is actively regulated by Ca2+ entry via voltage-gated Ca2+ channels and Ca2+ release from internal stores.
